There are approximately 40-45 million digital nomads worldwide, according to a 2026 report

According to an estimate based on the Nomads.com report "The 2026 State of Digital Nomads," there will be around 40-45 million digital nomads globally by 2026, and this number continues to grow. The typical representative of this group, based on user data from the platform, is a male aged 30-40 from North America or Europe, with an annual income ranging from $50,000 to $250,000.

The data comes from a report built on information about Nomads.com users. It indicates that the average digital nomad most often holds a bachelor's degree, works full-time or runs a startup, and does not identify as religious. The average age in the sample is about 37 years.

The report notes that a significant portion of the community consists of established professionals and entrepreneurs with relatively high incomes, rather than just young backpackers. At the same time, the ability to live and work from anywhere in the world is still not equally accessible to everyone. Popular cities among users include Bangkok, London, Barcelona, Paris, and New York.

⚖️ Crypto in 401(k)s: White House Review Is the Last Stop

The U.S. Department of Labor's rule on alternative assets in retirement plans landed at the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs on Thursday — the final regulatory checkpoint before public release. The rule would create a process-based safe harbor for plan fiduciaries who include crypto, private equity, and real estate in 401(k) menus, making it significantly easier for employers to offer that exposure without running afoul of fiduciary duty standards.

OIRA review typically signals a rule is close to finalization. Millions of American retirement accounts could soon have a clearer path to Bitcoin exposure — whether savers want that or not.

📌 Governance Snapshots: Why Your Tokens May Not Count in a DAO Vote

Main Points
⏺ Some DAOs calculate voting power using token balances from a specific blockchain block
⏺ Buying tokens after that snapshot may not increase your voting power
⏺ This post explains how balance snapshots work and why purchase timing matters

1️⃣ Core Idea — the protocol records balances at a selected block to determine how many votes each participant receives.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — a fixed reference point prevents voting power from changing every time tokens are transferred during the voting process.
3️⃣ Example — a vote uses balances from block #1000, but you buy tokens at block #1005. Those new tokens won't increase your voting power for that proposal.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — users may buy governance tokens specifically to participate, only to discover the snapshot already happened.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — before buying governance tokens, check the snapshot block, delegation conditions, and voting eligibility rules.

Final Thoughts

DAO governance isn't only about how many tokens you hold. It can also depend on when you held them. Sometimes your voting power is decided before the vote even begins.

🌐 Former FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.47M in crypto from 35 investigations 

🔔 Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency through nearly 100 unauthorized transfers linked to 35 federal investigations. Yaroch, who previously worked in the bureau’s counterintelligence division, faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted his guilty plea in Alexandria, Virginia, with sentencing scheduled for March 4, 2027.

📊 Court documents show that Yaroch worked at the FBI’s Boston Division between 2017 and early 2025, where he was assigned to a squad investigating an adversarial nation-state. He subsequently transferred to the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in February 2025, gaining access to FBI systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained during criminal and intelligence investigations. 

⚡️ Prosecutors said his thefts began no later than December 2024, before he moved to the new division. Using credentials associated with investigations outside his authorized activities, Yaroch accessed cryptocurrency wallets and transferred funds without permission. The approximately 100 fraudulent transactions involved credentials connected to 35 separate FBI investigations. Authorities calculated his total illicit proceeds at $2,474,380.66, substantially exceeding the roughly $1 million initially identified when his activities became public.
